subtopics.title: Operator Overloading
subtopics.subtitle: Giving C++ operators meaning for class types: member vs friend, unary, binary, =, [], ()

concepts.text: Purpose and Syntax

Operator overloading lets the built-in operators (+, -, ==, <<, [] and so on) work on objects of user-defined classes, so that c1 + c2 reads as naturally for two Complex numbers as it does for two ints. It is a form of compile-time polymorphism: the compiler picks the overload from the operand types. An overloaded operator is an ordinary function whose name is the keyword operator followed by the operator symbol. The compiler rewrites a + b as a.operator+(b) when the function is a member of the class, or as operator+(a, b) when it is a non-member function.
Rules every overload must obey:
items: You cannot invent new operators (no ** for power) and cannot redefine operators for built-in types alone: at least one operand must be a class or enumeration type.
Precedence, associativity and the number of operands (arity) are fixed: an overloaded * still binds tighter than +, and a binary + always takes exactly two operands.
Meaning is not enforced: operator+ may subtract, but good practice keeps the natural meaning of the symbol.
Five operators can never be overloaded: :: (scope resolution), . (member access), .* (pointer-to-member), ?: (conditional) and sizeof; typeid and the C++ cast operators are also excluded.
The operators =, [], () and -> must be member functions; every other overloadable operator may be a member or a non-member.
Default arguments are not allowed for overloaded operators, except for operator().

concepts.text: Member vs Friend (Non-member) Functions
Choosing the form:
items: Member function: the left operand is the object itself (*this), so a unary operator takes no parameter and a binary operator takes one.

Non-member function: all operands are parameters, so unary takes one parameter and binary takes two. Declare it friend inside the class if it must touch private data; otherwise it uses public getters.

Use a non-member when the left operand is not an object of your class: 2.0 * c needs operator*(double, const Complex&), and cout << c needs operator<<(ostream&, const Complex&) because the left operand is the stream.
A member overload never converts its left operand through a constructor, but a non-member converts either operand, which is why symmetric operators such as + and == are often written as friends.

rows: 2 parameters: T operator+(const T&, const T&)

concepts.text: Unary Operators: -, ++ and --

The prefix and postfix forms use the same symbol, so C++ tells them apart with an unused int parameter: operator++() is prefix and operator++(int) is postfix, and the compiler passes 0 as the dummy argument. Prefix should return a reference to the updated object (*this) so that ++(++c) works, while postfix must copy the old value, increment the object and return the copy by value, which is why postfix is slightly slower for class types. As friends the signatures are Counter& operator++(Counter& c) for prefix and Counter operator++(Counter& c, int) for postfix.
Binary Operators and Stream Insertion

Arithmetic operators build and return a new object by value, while comparison operators (==, !=, <, >) return bool; a magnitude-based operator< for Complex would compare re*re + im*im. The insertion operator << cannot be a member of Complex because its left operand is an ostream, so it is written as a friend taking (ostream&, const Complex&) and returning ostream& so that cout << a << b chains left to right. Extraction >> takes (istream&, Complex&), a non-const reference, because it modifies the object being read into.
Assignment, Subscript and Function Call
Return types and chaining:
items: Copy assignment, compound assignment (+=) and prefix ++ return T& (that is, *this) so calls can chain: a = b = c is evaluated as a = (b = c).
Arithmetic and postfix operators return a fresh T by value; returning a reference to a local object is a dangling-reference bug.
operator[] returns a reference so the element can be assigned to; add a const overload returning a value or const reference for const objects.
operator() may take any number of parameters, which lets an object behave like a function (a function object or functor), widely used with STL algorithms.
The compiler-generated operator= does a shallow member-wise copy; a class that owns heap memory must overload = together with the copy constructor and destructor (the rule of three) to deep copy.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Operator Overloading

For an expression a @ b the compiler collects three kinds of candidates: member functions a.operator@(b) of the left operand's class, non-member functions operator@(a, b) (friends declared in the class are found through the operands' class), and the built-in operator; ordinary overload resolution then picks the best match. A member candidate exists only when the left operand already is an object of the class, because no conversion is ever applied to the object that becomes *this, whereas a non-member lets both operands be converted by a converting constructor. That is why, with a constructor M(int), a member operator+ accepts a + 3 but rejects 3 + a, while a friend operator+ accepts both; marking the constructor explicit switches this conversion off.

concepts.plainText: a = b = c is evaluated as a.operator=(b.operator=(c)), so the inner call must return the object (normally T&, that is *this); a void return breaks the chain

concepts.text:
Worked example 1 - output: 7 5 7
Ctr a(5);      a.n = 5
b = a++;       postfix: old = copy of a (5); a.n = 6; b is the copy -> b.n = 5
c = ++a;       prefix:  a.n = 7; returns a itself; c copies it     -> c.n = 7
print          a.n = 7, b.n = 5, c.n = 7
The dummy int only selects the postfix version; the compiler passes 0.

Worked example 2 - output: [17][12][3]
c = 10 + a     int on the left: only the friend fits, 10 -> M(10)
               operator+(M(10), a) = M(12)                        c = 12
(a += b)       a.operator+=(b): a = 2 + 3 = 5, returns a (M&)
      += c     a.operator+=(c): a = 5 + 12 = 17                   a = 17
cout << a << c << b
               = operator<<(operator<<(operator<<(cout, a), c), b)
               each call returns cout, so the output is [17][12][3]

Relational operators are normally built from two primitives: define == and <, then write a != b as !(a == b), a > b as b < a, a <= b as !(b < a) and a >= b as !(a < b). In C++17 the compiler generates none of these, so a class with only operator== cannot be compared with !=. A class that overloads operator() produces function objects (functors); unlike a plain function, a functor can keep state in its data members between calls, and each copy of it keeps its own state.
Frequent errors in overloaded operators:
items: Returning a reference to a local result from operator+ (T& operator+(...) { T r; ...; return r; }): r dies at the closing brace, leaving a dangling reference.
Taking the right operand by non-const reference (T operator+(T &o)): then a + (b + c) fails because the temporary b + c cannot bind to T&.
Writing operator<< as a member function: it then has to be used as obj << cout, never cout << obj.
Returning void from operator= or operator<<: a single use works, but a = b = c and cout << x << y no longer compile.
Returning T& from postfix ++: the old value exists only as a local copy, so postfix must return T by value.
Defining both a member and a non-member version with the same parameter types, which makes every call ambiguous.

concepts.text: To trace an overloaded-operator program, first rewrite each operator as the call it becomes (a + b as a.operator+(b) or operator+(a, b), c++ as c.operator++(0)), keep the normal precedence and associativity, and note for each call whether it returns a copy or a reference to *this. Then evaluate the calls exactly like ordinary function calls.

Overloading &&, || or the comma operator turns them into ordinary function calls: both operands are always evaluated, so short-circuit evaluation is lost (C++17 still evaluates the left operand first). Avoid overloading these three.

formulas.plainText: a + b is a.operator+(b) for a member, operator+(a, b) for a non-member
For an n-operand operator: a member takes n - 1 parameters, a friend takes n
Prefix: T& operator++()  |  Postfix: T operator++(int) - the int is a dummy
Cannot be overloaded: ::  .  .*  ?:  sizeof

notes.text: operator++(int): the int is only a marker that means postfix. Prefix returns T&, postfix returns T holding the old value. For Counter d = c++; d keeps the value before the increment and c is incremented.
Without the if (this != &o) check, a deep-copying operator= applied to a = a deletes the data first and then copies from freed memory. Also remember to return *this, or a = b = c will not compile.

cout << obj works only with a non-member (usually friend) operator<< that returns ostream&. A member version would have to be called as obj << cout, because the left operand of a member operator is always *this.
Overloading never changes precedence, associativity or arity: in c1 + c2 * c3 the * runs first whatever your overloads do, and you cannot write a one-operand binary +.

formulas.title: Operator call rewriting
formulas.plainText: a + b is a.operator+(b) (member) or operator+(a, b) (non-member)
formulas.description: The compiler translates an operator expression into a call of the overloaded operator function.

formulas.title: Parameter count
formulas.plainText: member: n - 1 parameters, friend: n parameters (n = number of operands)
formulas.description: A member operator gets its left operand as *this, so unary members take 0 parameters and binary members take 1; friends take 1 and 2.

formulas.title: Prefix vs postfix increment
formulas.plainText: prefix: T& operator++()  |  postfix: T operator++(int)
formulas.description: The dummy int parameter distinguishes postfix from prefix; postfix returns the old value by value.

formulas.title: Non-overloadable operators
formulas.plainText: Cannot be overloaded: ::  .  .*  ?:  sizeof
formulas.description: These five operators (plus typeid and the cast operators) keep their built-in meaning; all others can be overloaded.

flashcards.front: How many parameters does a binary operator overloaded as a member function take?
flashcards.back: One, the right operand; the left operand is *this. As a friend or non-member it takes two.

flashcards.front: Why must operator<< for a class be a friend (non-member) function?
flashcards.back: Its left operand is an ostream, not an object of the class, and a member operator always has *this as the left operand. It returns ostream& so output chains.

flashcards.front: Which operators must be overloaded as member functions?
flashcards.back: Assignment =, subscript [], function call () and member access ->. All other overloadable operators may be members or non-members.

flashcards.front: What does an overloaded postfix operator++ return, and why?
flashcards.back: A copy of the object as it was before the increment, returned by value, because c++ evaluates to the old value. Prefix returns the updated object by reference.

questions.explanation: operator++(int) is the postfix form: it saves a copy t of the old object (n = 5), increments the original to 6 and returns the copy. So d.get() is 5 and c.get() is 6.

questions.questionText: Which of the following operators must be overloaded as a member function and cannot be written as a friend function?
questions.explanation: C++ requires =, [], () and -> to be member functions. +, == and << may be members or non-members (<< is normally a friend because its left operand is a stream).

questions.questionText: Postfix ++ is overloaded for class Counter as a non-member (friend) function. How many parameters does that function take?
questions.explanation: As a non-member, postfix ++ receives the object to change as Counter& plus a dummy int that marks the postfix form: friend Counter operator++(Counter &c, int). One parameter (Counter&) alone would declare the prefix form.

questions.questionText: A class overloads unary minus (-a) as a member function and binary minus (a - b) as a friend function. How many explicit parameters do the two functions take, respectively?
questions.explanation: A member operator receives its left (or only) operand as *this, so unary minus as a member takes 0 parameters. A friend has no this, so binary minus as a friend takes both operands explicitly: 2 parameters.

a + 3 becomes a.operator+(3), and 3 is converted to Num(3) by the constructor. In 3 + a the left operand is an int, and a member operator is only considered when an object of the class is on the left (no conversion is applied to it), so Line 2 finds no operator+.

options: Compile error: 3 + a has no matching operator
questions.explanation: A non-member operator lets either operand be converted, so a + 3 is operator+(a, Num(3)) = 2 * 10 + 3 = 23 and 3 + a is operator+(Num(3), a) = 3 * 10 + 2 = 32. The operands are never swapped.

questions.questionText: Class P overloads insertion as a member function: ostream& operator<<(ostream &os) const { return os << v; }. With P p; which expression compiles and prints p?
questions.explanation: For a member operator the left operand is always *this, so the expression must be p << cout, which becomes p.operator<<(cout). cout << p needs an operator whose left operand is an ostream, which only a non-member can supply.

questions.questionText: Which statement about operator overloading is NOT correct?
options: A friend operator function receives its left operand through the this pointer
At least one operand of an overloaded operator must be of a class or enumeration type
The compiler-generated operator= copies the object member by member
The dummy int parameter distinguishes postfix ++ from prefix ++
questions.explanation: A friend operator function is not a member, so it has no this pointer; it receives every operand as a parameter. The other three statements are standard rules of operator overloading.

questions.questionText: In the member declaration Counter operator++(int); what is the purpose of the int parameter?
options: It is the amount by which the object is incremented
It is the value that the operator must return
It makes the operator usable only on int members
It is an unused marker that tells the compiler this is the postfix form
questions.explanation: operator++(int) is the postfix form; the int only distinguishes it from the prefix operator++(). For c++ the compiler calls c.operator++(0), and the parameter is normally left unnamed and unused.
The friend with parameters (D &, int) is postfix --: it saves the old object, subtracts 2 from the original and returns the old copy. y = x-- gives y = 10 and x = 8; the second x-- makes x = 6.

operator++() returns C by value, so the inner ++c changes c to 2 but returns a copy; the outer ++ increments that copy to 3, and d is initialised from it. So c = 2 and d = 3; returning C& would have given 3 3.
a++ calls operator++(int): b gets the old value 4 and a becomes 4 + 3 = 7. ++a calls operator++(): a becomes 7 * 2 = 14 and c copies the updated object, 14.
-p calls operator-() and gives q = (-3, 5), so q.sum() = 2. !z is true because both members are 0, and !q is false; they print as 1 and 0, so the output is 2 10.
+ stays left-associative, so c = (a + b) + Cx(5). a + b = (4, 6), and Cx(5) is (5, 0) because im defaults to 0, giving (9, 6), printed as 9+6i.
An overloaded operator keeps the built-in associativity, so a - b - c means (a - b) - c = (10 - 3) - 2 = 5. The parentheses give 10 - (3 - 2) = 9.
Overloaded operators keep their built-in precedence, so a + b * c is a + (b * c) = 2 + 12 = 14, while (a + b) * c = 5 * 4 = 20.

a * 2 uses the member operator*(int): 3 * 2 + 1 = 7. 2 * a has an int on the left, so only the friend matches: 3 * 2 - 1 = 5. 2 * a * 2 is (2 * a) * 2: the friend gives 5, then the member gives 5 * 2 + 1 = 11.
Both operators compare total inches: a = 5*12 + 2 = 62, b = 4*12 + 14 = 62, c = 5*12 + 3 = 63. a == b is 1, a < c is 1 and c < b is 0, giving 110.

questions.questionText: Class Money overloads only bool operator==(const Money &) const. With Money a, b; which expression fails to compile under C++17?
questions.explanation: In C++17 the compiler does not derive != from ==; every relational operator that is used must be overloaded itself. a != b therefore has no matching operator, while the other expressions use only == and built-in bool operators.
The comparison uses only the last digit: 9 for a, 3 for b and 7 for c. a < b is 9 < 3 = 0; a > c is c < a, 7 < 9 = 1; b > c is c < b, 7 < 3 = 0: output 010.

a = b calls a.operator=(b) and works even though the result is void. In a = b = c the inner b = c yields void, and no operator= accepts a void argument, so Line 2 fails; operator= should return A& (*this).
Q c = a and Q d(b) create new objects, so they call the copy constructor (C). b = a and both assignments in d = c = a act on existing objects and call operator= (A). Order: C, A, C, A, A.

questions.questionText: Class Str holds char *p that points to memory obtained with new[], and its destructor does delete[] p. The class does not define operator=. After Str a("hi"), b("yo"); b = a; which statement is correct?
options: b.p and a.p now point to the same block, so it is deleted twice when a and b are destroyed, and b's original block leaks
b receives its own copy of the characters, because the default operator= performs a deep copy
b = a; does not compile, because no operator= is defined
Only the pointer is copied, but the compiler frees b's old block automatically first
questions.explanation: The compiler-generated operator= copies each member, so b.p simply receives a's address: b's own block is never freed and both destructors delete[] the same memory. A class owning heap memory needs a deep-copying operator= (rule of three).

questions.questionText: A deep-copying copy assignment operator begins with if (this != &o). What is the purpose of this test?
options: To make sure that o is not a null pointer
To allow chained assignments such as a = b = c
To skip freeing and re-copying the data when an object is assigned to itself, as in a = a
To check whether the two objects hold equal values
questions.explanation: In a = a, a deep-copying operator= would delete its own buffer and then copy from that freed memory. Comparing the addresses this and &o detects self-assignment so the work can be skipped; chaining depends on returning *this, not on this test.
operator= copies the pointed-to value (*p = *o.p), not the pointer, so a and b keep separate heap ints. After b = a, b holds 1; a.set(9) changes only a's int, so the output is 9 1.
c = a + b builds M(3) and then calls c.operator=, which stores 3 * 2 = 6. a = b = c runs right to left: b = c stores 6 * 2 = 12 and returns b, then a = b stores 24. Output 24 12 6.

operator+= returns *this by reference, so (m += 2) += 3 applies both additions to m itself: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6, and m += 4 gives 10. If it returned M by value, the + 3 would change only a temporary and the result would be 7.

questions.questionText: Why should an overloaded operator+ return its result by value rather than by reference?
options: The result is a new object created inside the function; a reference to that local object would dangle after the function returns
Returning by value is what lets a + b modify a
No operator function is allowed to return a reference
Returning by value automatically makes operator+ a member function
questions.explanation: a + b must leave both operands unchanged and produce a fresh value, which is a local object inside operator+. Returning a reference to it would refer to a destroyed object, so the result is returned by value; operators such as = and += do return references.

questions.questionText: Class Cx declares its addition operator as the member Cx operator+(Cx &o); (a non-const reference parameter in a non-const function). With Cx a, b, c, d; which statement fails to compile?
questions.explanation: b + c produces a temporary, and a temporary cannot bind to the non-const reference Cx&, so a + (b + c) fails. In a + b + c the temporary a + b is only the left operand, on which a member function may be called, and c is an ordinary object; a const Cx& parameter would fix the problem.
cout << a << "-" << b is evaluated left to right as ((cout << a) << "-") << b. The friend prints (1,2), then - is printed, then (3,4); each call returns the stream so the next << can use it.

questions.questionText: Why does an overloaded insertion operator return ostream& (for example ostream& operator<<(ostream &os, const Pt &p))?
options: Because every friend function must return a reference
So that the object p is modified while it is being printed
So that cout << a is the stream itself, which lets cout << a << b continue with the same stream
Because ostream objects are returned by value by default
questions.explanation: cout << a << b is parsed as (cout << a) << b, so the value of cout << a must be the stream to act as the left operand of the next <<. Returning the same ostream by reference does that; streams cannot even be copied, so returning by value would not compile.

This operator<< returns void. Line 1 does not use the result, and in Line 3 cout << "x" returns ostream& before the user operator is applied last, so both compile. In Line 2, (cout << a) is void, and void << b has no operator.

questions.questionText: Which declaration inside class Pt lets the statement cin >> p; read a value into a private member of the Pt object p?
questions.explanation: Extraction takes the input stream as its left operand and must change the object, so it is a non-member (friend) taking istream& and a non-const Pt&, returning istream& for chaining. A const Pt& cannot be written to, cin is not an ostream, and the member form would have to be used as p >> cin.

options: Compile error: src >> a >> b cannot be chained for class types
questions.explanation: Each call reads an int, the '/' into c and another int, then returns the stream, so src >> a >> b fills a = 3/4 and then b = 5/6. The program prints b first: 5/6 3/4.
operator[] returns int&, so x[i] can appear on either side of an assignment. x[1] = 7 + 8 = 15, then x[0] += 15 gives 5 + 15 = 20.

questions.questionText: Class Arr declares its subscript operator as int operator[](int i) const { return a[i]; } (it returns the element by value). With Arr x; which statement fails to compile?
questions.explanation: The operator returns a copy of the element, a temporary int, and a temporary cannot be assigned to. Reading x[i] works; returning int& (from a non-const operator[]) would make x[1] = 9 legal.

a is non-const, so a[2] uses the non-const operator[], which multiplies d[2] by 10: d = {1, 2, 30}. Inside show(), v is a const reference, so the const version is chosen and changes nothing: 1 + 2 + 30 = 33. a[1] then uses the non-const version, making d[1] = 20, which is printed.
f is a function object computing x*x + x + 1. f(0) = 1, f(2) = 4 + 2 + 1 = 7, and f(f(1)) = f(3) = 9 + 3 + 1 = 13.
s accumulates 4 and then 6, so r = 10. t is a copy of s made at that moment (total 10) and then adds 10 to reach 20, while s keeps its own total. s(0) returns 10 and t(0) returns 20.

questions.questionText: In C++17, which operator function may be declared with any number of parameters and may also have default arguments?
questions.explanation: operator() is the only operator that may take any number of parameters (including none) and may have default arguments. In C++17 operator[] takes exactly one parameter, operator-> takes none, and default arguments are not allowed on operator=.

questions.questionText: An object of a class that overloads the function-call operator operator() can be used as f(x). What is such an object called?
questions.explanation: Because it can be called like a function, an object whose class defines operator() is called a function object or functor; such objects are widely passed to STL algorithms.

questions.questionText: Operator overloading is an example of which kind of polymorphism?
options: Run-time polymorphism, resolved through virtual functions
It is not a form of polymorphism at all
questions.explanation: The compiler picks the operator function from the operand types while compiling, exactly as it does for overloaded functions, so operator overloading is compile-time (static) polymorphism. Run-time polymorphism needs virtual functions and base-class pointers or references.

questions.questionText: Which set contains ONLY operators that cannot be overloaded?
questions.explanation: The operators that can never be overloaded are :: . .* ?: and sizeof (plus typeid and the cast keywords). ->, [], (), ->*, new and delete are all overloadable, so each of the other sets contains at least one overloadable operator.

questions.questionText: Cx is a class. Which of these non-member operator declarations is a compile error?
questions.explanation: An overloaded operator must have at least one operand of class or enumeration type; operator+(int, int) would redefine addition of built-in ints, which is not allowed. Each of the other declarations has a Cx operand.

questions.questionText: A programmer wants a ** b to mean a raised to the power b for objects of class Big. How can this be achieved with operator overloading?
options: It cannot: only existing C++ operators can be overloaded, and ** is not a C++ operator
Declare Big operator**(const Big &b) const; as a member function
Declare friend Big operator**(const Big &a, const Big &b); in the class
Overload operator^, which C++ reserves as the power operator
questions.explanation: Overloading can only give new meaning to operators that already exist; C++ has no ** operator (a ** b would parse as a * (*b)), so operator** cannot be declared in any form. ^ is bitwise XOR, not power; a named function such as power(a, b) is the usual solution.

questions.questionText: When an operator is overloaded for a class, which of the following can the programmer change?
options: The action it performs on objects of the class
The number of operands it takes
questions.explanation: Overloading only supplies the function that runs when the operator is applied to objects of the class. Precedence, associativity and the number of operands are fixed by the language.

questions.questionText: Which of these member declarations inside class Cx is a compile error?
questions.explanation: Overloaded operator functions may not have default arguments; in C++17 the single exception is operator() (C++23 also allows them on operator[]). The default argument on operator+'s parameter is therefore an error, while operator() may use y = 1.

questions.questionText: A class overloads operator&& as a function taking two objects of the class. Which statement about an expression x && y that uses this overload is correct (C++17)?
options: The right operand is evaluated only if the left one is true, exactly as with the built-in &&
The overload must be declared as a member function
The overload is ignored and the built-in && is always used
Both operands are always evaluated, so short-circuit evaluation is lost
questions.explanation: An overloaded && is an ordinary function call, so both operands are evaluated before the function runs and short-circuiting is lost (C++17 still evaluates the left operand first). It may be declared as a member or a non-member.

subtopics.title: Data Conversion
subtopics.subtitle: Implicit and explicit conversions among basic types, and between basic and class types

concepts.text: Conversions Among Basic Types

C++ converts values between its built-in types automatically whenever an expression mixes types or a value is assigned to a variable of a different type; this is implicit conversion, also called coercion. The compiler follows fixed rules: in a mixed expression the smaller operand is promoted to the larger type so that no information is lost, while on assignment the value is converted to the type of the variable on the left even if that narrows it. An explicit conversion, or cast, is written by the programmer to force a particular conversion at a particular point.
Implicit conversion rules:
items: Integral promotion: bool, char and short are promoted to int before any arithmetic, so 'A' + 1 is the int 66, not a char.

Usual arithmetic conversions: if either operand is long double, double or float, the other is converted to that type; otherwise integer rank decides (int -> long -> long long), and unsigned wins over signed of the same rank.
Assignment conversion may narrow: int i = 3.9 stores 3 (truncation toward zero, not rounding), and char c = 300 keeps only the low 8 bits, which is 44.
Sub-expressions are evaluated before the assignment converts: double d = 7 / 2 gives 3.0 because 7 / 2 is already an integer division; write 7 / 2.0 to get 3.5.
Any arithmetic value converts to bool as non-zero = true; a pointer converts to bool as not-null.

concepts.text:
int i = 7;  double d = 2.0;  char ch = 'A';
cout << i / 2 << " " << i / d << "\n";    // 3 3.5  (int/int, then i promoted to double)
cout << ch + 1 << "\n";                   // 66     (char promoted to int)
int t = 3.99;                             // 3      (narrowing on assignment)
double a1 = (double)i / 2;                // 3.5    C-style cast
double a2 = double(i) / 2;                // 3.5    function-style cast
double a3 = static_cast<double>(i) / 2;   // 3.5    C++ cast, checked at compile time

rows: Works for almost anything, hard to search for, no compile-time checking
Same effect as the C-style cast; common in C++ textbooks
Compile-time checked conversion between related types; the preferred C++ form
Remove const, reinterpret the bit pattern, or safely downcast a polymorphic pointer

concepts.text: Basic Type to Class Type: the Constructor

A constructor that can be called with a single argument is a converting constructor: the compiler uses it automatically whenever an object of the class is required but a value of the argument type is supplied. Distance d = 2.5f; then d = 4.0f; and passing 2.5f to a function that takes a Distance all create a temporary Distance from the float through that constructor. Writing explicit in front of the constructor switches off this implicit use; the constructor then works only in direct form such as Distance d(2.5f), Distance(2.5f) or static_cast<Distance>(2.5f).
Class Type to Basic Type: the Conversion Operator

The reverse direction cannot use a constructor, because the destination type (float or double) is not a class and has no constructors. Instead the class defines a conversion function, also called a casting operator or conversion operator: operator float() const. It is a member function with no parameters and no declared return type, since the name already says what it returns. The compiler calls it whenever a Distance appears where a float is expected: float m = d; or 2 * d; or an explicit cast such as (float)d or static_cast<float>(d).
Class to Class Conversion
Converting an object of one class into an object of another can be written in either class:
items: Constructor in the destination class taking the source object: Fahrenheit(const Celsius& c). The destination must reach the source data through its public getters or by being a friend.
Conversion function in the source class: operator Fahrenheit() const written inside Celsius, which builds and returns the destination object.

Choose one place. If the destination has a converting constructor taking const Celsius& and the source has operator Fahrenheit() const, both are equally good for f = c or Fahrenheit f = c and the compiler reports an ambiguity error. (If the conversion function is not const and the source object is not const, the compiler prefers the conversion function — relying on that is fragile, so define only one.)
Only one user-defined conversion is applied automatically in a chain: the compiler will not silently go int -> Celsius -> Fahrenheit.

A conversion function cannot declare a return type and cannot take parameters, but it may be virtual and is inherited by derived classes.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Data Conversion

All the implicit rules follow one principle: in a mixed expression both operands are converted to a common type chosen from a fixed ranking, and only an assignment, a return statement, an argument pass or a cast may move a value to a narrower type. The integer ladder by rank is int, long, long long, and float, double and long double sit above every integer type. When a signed and an unsigned operand of the same rank meet, the signed one is converted to unsigned, so -1 becomes the largest unsigned value and -1 < 1u is false. Narrowing is accepted silently in an ordinary assignment, but C++11 brace initialisation such as int n{3.7}; rejects it at compile time.

subtopics.title: Inheritance: Types, Constructors & Destructors
subtopics.subtitle: Base/derived classes, access modes, six inheritance types, constructor/destructor order

concepts.text: Base and Derived Classes

Inheritance creates a new class (the derived class or subclass) from an existing one (the base class or superclass). The derived class receives all data members and member functions of the base and may add its own or redefine inherited ones; the relationship is is-a (a Circle is a Shape). The benefits are code reuse, a natural class hierarchy, and the ability to handle derived objects through base pointers, which is the basis of the polymorphism covered in the next subtopic. The syntax is class Derived : access-mode Base { ... }; where the access mode (public, protected or private) controls how the inherited members appear inside the derived class.
What a derived class does NOT inherit:
items: Constructors and the destructor: each class writes its own, and the derived constructor calls a base constructor (C++11 can import base constructors with using Base::Base).
The copy-assignment operator= of the base, and the friend functions and friend classes of the base.
Private members are physically inherited (they exist inside every derived object and count in sizeof) but cannot be accessed by name from the derived class.
A function redefined in the derived class hides all base overloads of that name; use Base::name() to reach the base version.

concepts.text: Access Modes

Public inheritance keeps the base interface public and models is-a; it is the only mode in which a Derived* converts implicitly to Base* outside the class. Protected inheritance turns base public members into protected ones, and private inheritance makes everything private, so a class derived further down can no longer see them. If no mode is written, class defaults to private inheritance and struct to public. A private base member is always out of reach by name; the derived class must go through the base's public or protected functions.

items: In the diamond, D receives one A sub-object through B and another through C, so d.x is ambiguous and A's constructor runs twice for one D.

The keyword virtual is written in B and C (the classes that share the base), not in D.

The order in class C : public A, public B fixes the order of base construction and the layout of the base sub-objects; multiple inheritance of classes is specific to C++ (Java allows it only through interfaces).

concepts.text: Constructors and Destructors in Inheritance

Constructors are not inherited, but creating a derived object always constructs its base part first: the base constructor runs, then the derived class's own member objects are initialised, and finally the body of the derived constructor executes (top-down). Destructors run in exactly the reverse order: the derived destructor body first, then the base destructor (bottom-up), so each class cleans up only what it built. In a multilevel chain A -> B -> C, creating a C runs A's, B's, then C's constructor, and destroying it runs ~C, ~B, ~A. If the base has no default (no-argument) constructor, the derived constructor must pass arguments to it explicitly in its initialiser list.
Order rules to remember:
items: Single inheritance: Base constructor -> Derived constructor; Derived destructor -> Base destructor.
Multilevel: grandparent -> parent -> child for constructors, and the exact reverse for destructors.

Multiple inheritance: base constructors run in the order the bases are listed in the class header, not the order written in the initialiser list; virtual base classes are constructed before all others.
Member objects are constructed after the base classes and before the derived constructor body, in their declaration order, and destroyed in reverse.
Make the base destructor virtual when objects are deleted through base pointers; otherwise only the base destructor runs, which is undefined behaviour.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Construction Order, Access and Name Hiding

The complete construction rule has four steps, applied recursively to every sub-object. First the virtual base classes are built, depth-first and left to right, and only by the most-derived class; then the direct non-virtual bases in the order of the class header; then the data members in their order of declaration; and finally the constructor body runs. The member-initialiser list only supplies arguments and never changes this order. Destruction walks the same list backwards, so every part is destroyed while the parts it depends on still exist.

Diamond A-B-C-D: D holds 2 copies of A normally, 1 copy with virtual base classes

notes.text: Constructor-order questions: write the chain top-down for construction (A B C) and reverse it for destruction (C B A). For multiple inheritance the order follows the class header, not the initialiser list.

class D : public B, public C where B and C both derive non-virtually from A gives two copies of A: d.x is a compile-time ambiguity error, not a runtime bug. The fix, virtual public A, goes on B and C, not on D.
Under private inheritance a Derived* no longer converts to Base* outside the class, and a class derived further from Derived cannot access any base member at all.
If the base has only a parameterised constructor and the derived constructor does not name it in the initialiser list, compilation fails with "no matching function for call to Base::Base()".

formulas.title: Inheritance syntax
formulas.latex: \text{class D : mode B1, mode B2 \{ \};}\quad \text{mode = public | protected | private}
formulas.plainText: class Derived : access-mode Base1, access-mode Base2 { };
formulas.description: One base gives single inheritance; a comma-separated list gives multiple inheritance; the mode defaults to private for class and public for struct.

formulas.title: Constructor and destructor order
formulas.plainText: Constructors: Base then Derived; destructors: Derived then Base
formulas.description: Construction is top-down and destruction is bottom-up, in single and multilevel inheritance alike.

formulas.title: Diamond sub-object count
formulas.plainText: Diamond: 2 copies of the top base without virtual, 1 copy with virtual base class
formulas.description: Virtual inheritance in the intermediate classes collapses the duplicated base into one shared sub-object.

formulas.title: Calls in a multilevel chain
formulas.latex: n\text{-level chain} \Rightarrow n \text{ ctor calls},\ n \text{ dtor calls}
formulas.plainText: n classes in a chain: n constructor calls and n destructor calls per object
formulas.description: Every level of a multilevel hierarchy contributes exactly one constructor and one destructor call for each object created.

flashcards.front: Which members are never inherited by a derived class?
flashcards.back: Constructors, the destructor, the copy-assignment operator and the friends of the base. Private members are inherited but inaccessible by name.
A base A with two derived classes B and C that are both bases of D; D reaches A by two paths and holds two copies of A unless B and C inherit A as a virtual base class.

flashcards.front: How does a derived constructor pass arguments to the base constructor?
flashcards.back: Through its member-initialiser list: Derived(int a, int b) : Base(a), member(b) { }. Required whenever the base has no default constructor.

flashcards.front: In what order are base constructors called for class C : public A, public B?
flashcards.back: A then B, following the order in the class header regardless of the initialiser-list order, and then C's own constructor body.

questions.explanation: Creating q runs the base constructor first (P) and then the derived one (Q). The dash is printed while q is alive, and at the end of main the destructors run in reverse: ~Q, then ~P.
c is destroyed when its inner block closes, before the ! is printed. In the multilevel chain A -> B -> C the destructors run bottom-up: ~C, ~B, then ~A.
The construction order is base class, then member objects, then the constructor body: A, M, B. Destruction is the exact reverse: the body of ~B, then the member (m), then the base (a).
Base classes are constructed in the order they are listed in the class header, struct Z : Y, X, whatever the order of the initialiser list. So Y(2) runs first, then X(1), then the body of Z.
Construction: the bases in header order X then Y, then the member extra (another Y), then the body Z, giving XYYZ. Destruction reverses it: z, the member y, the base Y (y), and finally x.

options: Compile error: C cannot access the protected member a
questions.explanation: C passes x and y up to B, and B passes x on to A, so a = 1, b = 2 and c = 3. Protected members stay accessible down a chain of public inheritance, and 1 * 100 + 2 * 10 + 3 = 123.

options: It compiles, and Base(int) is called with the value 0
It compiles, and the Base part of d is left unconstructed
It compiles but fails at run time when d is created
Compile error: Base has no default constructor and Der() does not call Base(int)
questions.explanation: Every derived constructor must construct its base part; when the initialiser list names no base constructor, the compiler calls Base(), which does not exist here. Writing Der() : Base(0) {} fixes the error.

questions.questionText: Class B has a protected data member x. Class D is derived privately from B, and class E is derived publicly from D. Which statement is correct?
options: Both D's and E's member functions can use x
D's member functions can use x, but E's member functions cannot
Neither D's nor E's member functions can use x
E's member functions can use x, but D's cannot
questions.explanation: Private inheritance turns the protected x into a private member of D, so D can still use it in its own functions. Private members of D are out of reach for E, even though E derives publicly from D.

A private member of the base is present in every B object but cannot be accessed by name in B, so x = 10 is an error. The protected y is usable inside B, and the public z stays public under public inheritance, so main can assign b.z.

Protected inheritance makes p and q protected in B, and they stay protected in C, so set() may use them but main may not write c.p. The conversion from B* to A* is also inaccessible in main, because A is a protected base of B, so lines 3 and 4 fail.
In hierarchical inheritance every derived object contains its own Counter sub-object; nothing is shared between l and r. l.n is incremented twice (2) and r.n once (1), so the output is 21.
Each base in the list takes its own access mode, and a base written without one is inherited privately by a class. So A is a public base but B is a private base, and c.fb() is inaccessible in main.

questions.questionText: Class B is derived from A, and class C is derived from B, so B is both a derived class and a base class. What type of inheritance is this?
questions.explanation: A chain A -> B -> C in which each class has one direct base is multilevel inheritance. Multiple inheritance would need one class with two or more direct bases.

questions.questionText: Classes Car, Bus and Truck are each derived only from class Vehicle. What type of inheritance is this?
questions.explanation: One base class with several derived classes is hierarchical inheritance. Multiple inheritance is the opposite shape (several bases, one derived), and multipath needs a class that reaches the same base by two paths.

questions.questionText: Class Test is derived from Student, and class Result is derived from both Test and Sports. What type of inheritance does this hierarchy show?
questions.explanation: Student -> Test -> Result is a multilevel chain, and Result also has two direct bases, Test and Sports, which is multiple inheritance. A combination of two or more types in one hierarchy is hybrid inheritance.
The bases of Result are built in header order: first Test, which builds Student before its own body (St Te), then Sports (Sp). The body of Result runs last (Re).

options: Compile error: Der::show() hides Base::show(int), so no visible show takes an int
It prints Der followed by Base 5
questions.explanation: Declaring any function named show in Der hides every Base function of that name, whatever its parameters. Name lookup stops in Der, finds only show(), and the call with an argument fails; d.Base::show(5) or using Base::show; would fix it.

using Base::show brings both base overloads into Der, but Der's own show(int) replaces the base one with the same signature. So d.show(1) calls Der's version, d.show(2.5) picks Base::show(double), and the qualified call d.Base::show(3) runs the base int version.
speak() is not virtual, so p->speak() is bound at compile time from the pointer's type, Animal*, and prints the three dots. Called on the Dog object itself, the derived version runs and prints Woof.

run() is inherited from A, and inside A's code the call who() means this->who() with this of type A*, bound at compile time to A::who. Only the direct call b.who() finds B's version, so the output is AB; with a virtual who() it would be BB.

r.draw() runs Ring::draw, which first calls Circle::draw (prints C, then Shape::draw prints S) and then prints R. p->draw() is not virtual and uses the pointer type Shape*, printing S, so the output is CSRS.
Without virtual base classes, B and C each contain their own A sub-object. Building D builds B (A then B), then C (A then C), then D's body, so A's constructor runs twice.

A virtual base is constructed once, by the most-derived class, before any non-virtual base. D's constructor does not name A, so A's default constructor A(0) runs, and the A(1) and A(2) initialisers in B and C are ignored when a D is built.
A D object contains two A sub-objects, so both the unqualified name x and the conversion from D* to A* are ambiguous. Qualifying with B:: or C:: selects one copy, so only lines 3 and 4 fail.

questions.questionText: In the diamond A -> B, A -> C, (B, C) -> D, where must the keyword virtual be written so that a D object contains only one A sub-object?
options: In the base list of D: class D : virtual public B, virtual public C
In the base lists of B and C: class B : virtual public A and class C : virtual public A
In front of every member function of A
In front of A's constructor: virtual A()
questions.explanation: The classes that share the base, B and C, must both declare A as a virtual base. Marking the bases of D virtual does not merge the two A copies, virtual member functions are unrelated to this, and a constructor cannot be virtual.
In hierarchical inheritance each derived object has its own base part. s builds Account(100) and then Saving, and then c builds Account(500) and then Current.
Local objects are destroyed in reverse order of creation, so y goes first. For each object ~D prints d before ~B prints the stored character, giving d2 and then d1.

questions.questionText: Which of the following does a derived class inherit from its public base class and can use directly by name?
options: The constructors of the base (without a using-declaration)
The public member functions of the base
The friend functions of the base
The private data members of the base
questions.explanation: Public and protected members are inherited and usable in the derived class. Constructors are not inherited unless imported with using Base::Base, friendship is not inherited, and private members exist in the object but cannot be named.

questions.questionText: How does a protected member of a class differ from a private member?
options: A protected member can be accessed from main() through an object, but a private one cannot
Member functions of a derived class can access a protected member, but not a private one
A protected member is not inherited, but a private one is
There is no difference: protected is another name for private
questions.explanation: Both are hidden from outside code such as main(). The difference appears only with inheritance: protected members are accessible inside derived classes, while private members are accessible only inside the class itself and its friends.
C(3) passes 3 * 2 = 6 to B, and B(6) passes 6 + 1 = 7 to A. The constructor bodies then run from the top of the chain down: A prints 7, B prints 6 and C prints 3.

options: Compile error: inc() is not a member of Der
questions.explanation: Der publicly inherits x and inc() from Base, so d.inc() works on d's own copy of x. Two increments make x = 7, and 7 + 10 = 17.

options: Compile error: n is protected in Base
questions.explanation: A protected member is accessible inside the member functions of a publicly derived class. twice() reads the inherited n = 4 and returns 4 * 2 = 8; only a direct access such as d.n in main would fail.

options: Compile error: the initialisers must follow the order of the base list
questions.explanation: Arguments reach each base constructor through the initialiser list; writing Width before Length is legal (at most a warning), and the bases are still built as Length and then Width. So l = 4, w = 6 and the area is 4 * 6 = 24.
Under private inheritance power() becomes private in Car: Car's own member hp() may call it, and main may call the public hp(). Calling c.power() from main is an access error, so only line 3 fails.

questions.questionText: Under public inheritance, what happens to a private data member of the base class?
options: It is present in every derived object but cannot be accessed by name in the derived class
It becomes a private member of the derived class that the derived class can access directly
It becomes a protected member of the derived class
It is not stored in derived objects at all
questions.explanation: Private members are inherited physically, so they occupy space in each derived object, but access to them is limited to the base class and its friends. The derived class must use the base's public or protected functions to reach them.
A Der object contains a complete Base sub-object, including the private members a and b (8 bytes), plus its own member c. So sizeof(Der) = 8 + 4 = 12 bytes, even though Der cannot name a or b.

options: Compile error: a Der object cannot initialise a Base object
questions.explanation: A derived object can initialise a base object, but only the Base part is copied (object slicing), so b.v is 7 and w is dropped. b is a genuine Base, so b.show() calls Base::show and prints Base7.

questions.questionText: Which declaration makes class Car publicly derived from class Vehicle in C++?
questions.explanation: C++ writes the base list after a single colon, with each base preceded by its access mode. extends is Java syntax, and :: is the scope resolution operator, not a base-list separator.

questions.questionText: Public inheritance is the right design when the relationship between the derived class and the base class is:
options: uses-a (a Printer uses a Document during one call)
part-of (a Wheel is part of a Car)
questions.explanation: Public inheritance means a derived object can be used wherever a base object is expected, which is the is-a relationship. has-a and part-of are modelled by member objects (composition), and uses-a by a function parameter.
Virtual bases are constructed first even when listed later, so V precedes B1; then come the member (M) and the body (D), giving V1MD. Destruction is the exact reverse: d, m, ! (for B1) and finally v.

questions.questionText: Which statement about constructors in inheritance is correct?
options: A derived constructor must always call a base constructor explicitly in its initialiser list
The base constructor runs after the body of the derived constructor
If the derived constructor names no base constructor, the base's default constructor is called automatically before the derived body
A derived class inherits the base's constructors automatically, so it never needs its own
questions.explanation: The base part is always built first; when the initialiser list names no base constructor, Base() is used, and an explicit call is required only if Base() does not exist. Constructors are not inherited unless they are imported with using Base::Base.

options: Compile error: Der has no constructor that takes an int
questions.explanation: Since C++11, the declaration using Base::Base; makes the base constructors usable as constructors of Der. Der d(4) therefore runs Base(4), which stores 4 * 10 = 40.
new B runs the constructors base first (AB), and delete p, through a B*, runs ~B and then ~A (ba) at that moment. The local obj is then built (A) and destroyed automatically when main returns (a).

questions.questionText: Classes A and B both define a public member function void show(), and class C : public A, public B does not redefine it. What happens for the call c.show(), where c is a C object?
options: A::show() runs because A is listed first
B::show() runs because the last base listed takes priority
Compile error: the call is ambiguous; write c.A::show() or c.B::show()
Both run, first A::show() and then B::show()
questions.explanation: Name lookup finds show in two different base classes, so the unqualified call is ambiguous at compile time; the order of the base list gives no priority. Qualifying the call, or redefining show() in C, resolves it.
